title: Endocrine Axes and How to Test Them

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In an anterior-pituitary axis, a {{c1::trophic hormone}} is the pituitary hormone that drives a target gland, such as ACTH driving the adrenal cortex.
cards.back: The target hormone is what that gland makes, such as cortisol.
cards.quote: A trophic hormone is the pituitary hormone that drives that gland, such as ACTH.

cards.front: When a target hormone and its trophic hormone are read together, which direction pattern points to a failed target gland, and which to failed drive from above?
cards.back: Opposite directions: the target gland failed. Same direction: the pituitary or hypothalamus failed.
cards.why: With the gland at fault, feedback still works, so the pituitary pushes against it. With the drive at fault, the gland simply follows.
cards.quote: If the fault is in the target gland, feedback still works, so the pituitary pushes against it and the two hormones move in opposite directions.

cards.front: Under what conditions does the paired trophic-target hormone rule hold, and which pituitary hormone does it not apply to?
cards.back: Once the axis has settled, for free hormone, in a sample timed to the hormone's rhythm, on an assay whose number means what you think. It does not apply to prolactin.
cards.quote: The rule holds once the axis has settled, for free hormone, in a sample timed to the hormone's rhythm

cards.front: For the ACTH, TSH and GH axes, name the main hypothalamic releasing hormone and the target-gland product.
cards.back: ACTH: CRH (helped by vasopressin), product cortisol. TSH: TRH, product T4 and T3. GH: GHRH (opposed by somatostatin), product IGF-1 from the liver.
cards.quote: CRH (corticotropin-releasing hormone), helped by vasopressin from the same hypothalamic neurons, drives ACTH
cards.section: One chain, three links, one feedback loop

cards.front: Hypothalamic {{c1::dopamine}} tonically inhibits prolactin release through lactotroph D2 receptors.
cards.back: No releasing hormone dominates prolactin control; the axis runs on a brake.
cards.quote: Hypothalamic dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release through lactotroph D2 receptors.
cards.section: One chain, three links, one feedback loop

cards.front: Why does IGF-1 not carry every effect of growth hormone?
cards.back: GH also acts directly through its own receptors, for example promoting breakdown of stored fat in adipose tissue.
cards.quote: GH also acts directly through its own receptors, for example promoting breakdown of stored fat in adipose tissue
cards.section: One chain, three links, one feedback loop

cards.front: Most releasing and pituitary hormones act on G protein-coupled receptors. Which two pituitary hormones are the exceptions, and through what do their receptors signal?
cards.back: GH and prolactin; their receptors signal through JAK2 and STAT5 (JAK-STAT).
cards.quote: GH and prolactin are the exceptions: their receptors signal through JAK2 and STAT5 (JAK-STAT).
cards.section: One chain, three links, one feedback loop

cards.front: What two jobs does a trophic hormone such as ACTH do for its gland?
cards.back: It tells the gland to secrete now, and over weeks it keeps the gland's secreting cells from shrinking.
cards.why: Take ACTH away for weeks and the cortisol-making layers of the adrenal cortex shrink, which shapes how stimulation tests read.
cards.quote: Over weeks it also keeps the gland's secreting cells from shrinking
cards.section: One chain, three links, one feedback loop

cards.front: What is long-loop feedback? Give the three anterior-pituitary examples with strong evidence.
cards.back: The target hormone travels back and restrains the links above it: cortisol on CRH and ACTH, T4 and T3 on TRH and TSH, IGF-1 on GH.
cards.quote: The target hormone travels back and restrains the links above it
cards.section: One chain, three links, one feedback loop

cards.front: Why does intact feedback make a trophic hormone level informative about its target gland?
cards.back: An intact pituitary keeps reading the target hormone, so the trophic hormone is a running report on its target.
cards.quote: an intact pituitary keeps reading the target hormone, so the trophic hormone is a running report on its target
cards.section: One chain, three links, one feedback loop

cards.front: Define primary, secondary, tertiary and central endocrine disorders.
cards.back: Primary: the target gland fails. Secondary: the pituitary fails. Tertiary: the hypothalamus fails. Central: secondary and tertiary together.
cards.quote: In a primary disorder the target gland itself fails.
cards.section: Which link failed? Read the pair

cards.front: Two adults, sampled at 08:00 and on no glucocorticoid medicine, both have low cortisol. One has very high ACTH; the other has low ACTH. Where has each chain failed?
cards.back: Very high ACTH: primary adrenal insufficiency. Low ACTH: central (pituitary or hypothalamus).
cards.why: Opposite directions mean the pituitary drives hard and the adrenal does not answer. Same direction means the adrenal gets almost no signal.
cards.quote: A: low cortisol, very high ACTH. The two move in opposite directions.
cards.section: Three mornings

cards.front: Low cortisol with low ACTH points to central adrenal insufficiency. Why can this pair not say whether the pituitary or the hypothalamus failed?
cards.back: Either lesion lowers ACTH, so both give the same same-direction pattern.
cards.quote: The pair cannot say whether it is the pituitary (secondary) or the hypothalamus (tertiary), because either lesion lowers ACTH.
cards.section: Three mornings

cards.front: Cortisol's molar mass is about 362.5 g per mol. Show that 1 µg per dL is about 27.6 nmol per L, then convert the historical cosyntropin criterion of 18 µg per dL.
cards.quote: Its molar mass is about 362.5 g per mol, so 1 µg per dL = 10 µg per L
cards.section: Three mornings

cards.front: An adult has an 08:00 cortisol of 14 µg per dL with ACTH in the usual morning range, but adrenal insufficiency is suspected. Does this pair prove normal adrenal reserve?
cards.back: No. It shows nothing has failed at rest, but a resting pair cannot show how the axis would cope with stress; that needs a dynamic test.
cards.quote: A resting pair cannot show how the axis would cope with stress
cards.section: Three mornings

cards.front: What does "inappropriately normal" mean for a trophic hormone, and why is it read the same as low?
cards.back: A trophic hormone inside the reference interval while its target is low has failed to rise; an intact pituitary should be driving hard.
cards.why: A reference interval comes from people with a normal target hormone, so judge a trophic hormone against its own target.
cards.quote: An ACTH that sits in the normal range while cortisol is low has failed to rise.
cards.section: "Inappropriately normal"

cards.front: Why is TSH alone a good first screen for primary hypothyroidism, yet a TSH-only screen misses central hypothyroidism?
cards.back: A small fall in free T4 brings a much larger proportional rise in TSH. In central disease TSH is usually low or inappropriately normal, so free T4 must be measured too.
cards.quote: a small fall in free T4 brings a much larger proportional rise in TSH
cards.section: The thyroid reads the same way

cards.front: A patient has high cortisol and high ACTH. What does the pair say, and what can it not say?
cards.back: Same direction with both high: excess drive from above, as in an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour (Cushing disease). It cannot say where the ACTH comes from: an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumour gives the same pattern.
cards.quote: It cannot split pituitary from hypothalamus, or pituitary ACTH from an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumour elsewhere in the body.
cards.section: When the pair rule is silent or fooled

cards.front: A patient has high free T4 and a suppressed TSH. Where does the pair point, and what is one cause that fits?
cards.back: Opposite directions with the target high: the thyroid is working on its own. Graves disease fits, where an antibody stimulates the thyroid's TSH receptor.
cards.why: The pituitary is obeying feedback and shutting TSH down.
cards.quote: Graves disease, where an antibody stimulates the thyroid's TSH receptor
cards.section: Excess reads the same way

cards.front: What question does a stimulation test ask of an endocrine gland, and what question does a suppression test ask?
cards.back: Stimulation: reserve, can the gland respond? Suppression: autonomy, does secretion still fall when the signals that normally turn it down are applied?
cards.quote: Stimulation tests ask about reserve: can this gland respond?
cards.section: Change one input: stimulation and suppression tests

cards.front: A patient's pituitary stopped making ACTH one week ago. A cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH) test gives a normal cortisol rise. What does the result show?
cards.back: Only that the adrenal can answer ACTH today. The cortex has not had time to shrink, so a recent pituitary or hypothalamic defect is not excluded.
cards.quote: So a normal response shows only that the adrenal can answer ACTH today.
cards.section: Change one input: stimulation and suppression tests

cards.front: Why can a cortisol of 16 µg per dL after cosyntropin pass on one assay yet fail against the historical criterion?
cards.back: The historical 18 µg per dL came from older, less specific immunoassays. Newer specific assays read lower on the same blood, and their criteria are about 14 to 15 µg per dL.
cards.quote: Newer, more specific assays read lower on the same blood, and the criteria derived for them in 2021 are lower
cards.section: Change one input: stimulation and suppression tests

cards.front: After a night-time dose of dexamethasone, next-morning cortisol fails to fall. What does this suggest, and what can it not show?
cards.back: Secretion escaping feedback. It does not locate the source, and faster dexamethasone clearance or more binding globulin can confound it.
cards.quote: Failure to suppress suggests secretion escaping feedback, but it does not locate the source.
cards.section: The other dynamic tests

cards.front: One patient takes a D2-blocking antipsychotic; another has a non-secreting mass compressing the pituitary stalk. Both have raised prolactin that falls on a D2 agonist. Does the drug response locate the problem, and what would point to the stalk?
cards.back: No: a D2 agonist lowers prolactin whether the cause is a stalk lesion or a prolactinoma, so the drug response does not locate the problem. A modest prolactin rise together with low levels of other pituitary hormones points to the stalk.
cards.quote: What points to the stalk is a modest prolactin rise together with low levels of other pituitary hormones.
cards.section: Test the wiring: a compressed stalk

cards.front: Why does prolactin sit outside the paired trophic-target hormone rule?
cards.back: It has no target hormone to pair with, and its hypothalamic control is a brake (dopamine), so losing hypothalamic input raises it.
cards.quote: it has no target hormone to pair with, and its hypothalamic control is a brake
cards.section: Test the wiring: a compressed stalk

cards.front: A non-secreting mass reduces portal delivery from the hypothalamus. Predict the free T4 and TSH pair, and explain why TSH need not be high even though free T4 is low.
cards.back: Free T4 tends to fall, with TSH low or inappropriately normal (combinations vary by patient): a same-direction, central pattern.
cards.why: TSH depends on TRH arriving in portal blood. With drive lost, the pituitary cannot push against low T4, so the pair rule reads it as missing drive.
cards.quote: TSH may be low or inappropriately normal rather than high.
cards.section: Test the wiring: a compressed stalk

cards.front: In young adults, when does the night's large GH surge come, and is it tied to clock time or to sleep?
cards.back: At the onset of deep (slow-wave) sleep. It is tied to sleep onset, not clock time.
cards.quote: the surge was tied to sleep onset, not clock time
cards.section: Condition 1: catch the right moment

cards.front: In humans on a usual sleep-wake schedule, when does the HPA axis peak and when does it reach its nadir?
cards.back: Peak between 06:00 and 10:00; nadir between 22:00 and 02:00, with ACTH and cortisol pulses on that curve.
cards.quote: it peaks between 06:00 and 10:00 and reaches its nadir between 22:00 and 02:00
cards.section: Condition 1: catch the right moment

cards.front: In a made-up model, a GH pulse peaks at 12 ng per mL and secretion then stops. Clearance is first order with a 27-minute half-life. What does plasma GH read 54 minutes after the peak?
cards.back: 54 / 27 = 2 half-lives, so 12 x 2^-2 = 3.0 ng per mL, a quarter of the peak.
cards.quote: a pulse decays to a quarter or less within an hour
cards.section: Condition 1: catch the right moment

cards.front: Why is a single random GH value in an adult weak evidence of GH deficiency?
cards.back: GH is pulsatile and cleared fast, so the sample may fall between pulses and read many-fold lower than one drawn on a peak.
cards.quote: a sample drawn just before a pulse can read many-fold lower than one drawn on its peak
cards.section: Condition 1: catch the right moment

cards.front: Why is TSH measured with a two-site (sandwich) immunoassay, while free T4 is usually measured competitively?
cards.back: A sandwich needs two antibodies bound to two sites on one molecule, which suits large peptides like TSH. T4 is too small for two antibodies to bind at once.
cards.quote: a small molecule is too small for two antibodies to bind it at once
cards.section: Condition 2: know what the assay measured

cards.front: In a two-site (sandwich) immunoassay, measured signal {{c1::rises}} as hormone concentration rises.
cards.back: In a competitive assay, bound signal falls as hormone rises.
cards.quote: In a two-site (sandwich) assay, a capture antibody and a signal antibody bind two sites on one molecule, so signal rises with hormone.
cards.section: Condition 2: know what the assay measured

cards.front: A reported prolactin is high, but most of it is macroprolactin. Why might it mean little at the receptor?
cards.back: Immunoassays measure immunoreactivity, not bioactivity. Macroprolactin, a large prolactin-IgG complex, is detected but has low biological activity.
cards.quote: Macroprolactin, a large prolactin-IgG complex, is detected by immunoassays but has low biological activity
cards.section: Condition 2: know what the assay measured

cards.front: What does LC-MS/MS offer over an immunoassay for hormones such as steroids?
cards.back: It separates the hormone from its relatives and identifies it by mass and fragments, so it reports a defined chemical species rather than antibody cross-reactivity.
cards.quote: separates the hormone from its relatives and identifies it by mass and fragments, so it reports a defined chemical species
cards.section: Condition 2: know what the assay measured

cards.front: A woman with a healthy thyroid starts oral estrogen, which raises thyroxine-binding globulin. Predict total T4, free T4 and TSH.
cards.back: Total T4 rises; free T4 stays near its usual range; TSH stays normal.
cards.why: Free hormone is the part available to tissues and the part feedback reads. With total T4 the pair rule seems broken; with free T4 it holds.
cards.quote: more thyroxine-binding globulin, as with oral estrogen, raises total T4 while free T4 stays near its usual range and TSH stays normal
cards.section: Condition 2: know what the assay measured

cards.front: A patient taking a biotin supplement has low TSH and high free T4 on a biotin-streptavidin platform. Design checks to tell an assay artefact from real hyperthyroidism.
cards.back: Rerun the sample on a platform without a biotin capture step; repeat after stopping biotin; look for physiological agreement such as heart rate, symptoms and T3 on a non-biotin platform.
cards.why: A biological change appears on both platforms and persists; an artefact appears only on the susceptible one and clears after washout.
cards.quote: Rerun the same sample on a platform without a biotin capture step: a biological change should appear on both, an artefact only on the susceptible one.
cards.section: The biotin study

cards.front: Ten days after pituitary surgery, morning cortisol is low, ACTH is low-normal, and a cosyntropin test is normal. Is the axis shown to be intact?
cards.back: No. The pair is same-direction (ACTH inappropriately normal), so drive looks inadequate. Ten days is too short for the cortex to shrink, so the normal test shows only that the adrenal works today. Repeat stimulation weeks later.
cards.why: Combines the pair rule with the trophic role of ACTH: a stimulation test detects lost drive only after the cortex has had time to shrink.
cards.quote: Ten days is too short for the adrenal cortex to have shrunk, so a normal response shows only that the adrenal works today.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Distinguish short-loop from ultra-short feedback in a hypothalamic-pituitary axis.
cards.back: Short-loop: a pituitary hormone acting back on the hypothalamus. Ultra-short: a hormone acting back on the very cells that make it, classically a releasing hormone on its own neurons.
cards.quote: Ultra-short feedback is a hormone acting back on the very cells that make it
cards.section: Short and ultra-short loops

cards.front: Female mice lacking prolactin receptors had more hyperprolactinemia than age-matched D2-receptor knockouts. What does this suggest, and what limits the inference?
cards.back: If prolactin restrained lactotrophs only by driving dopamine, losing its receptor could at most match losing D2. Doing worse points to a second restraint not running through dopamine.
cards.why: Limits: the knockouts differ in other ways (infertility, steroid milieu), deletions are global and lifelong, and results are mainly in females.
cards.quote: Doing worse than the D2 knockout therefore points to a second restraint that does not run through dopamine
cards.section: Short and ultra-short loops

cards.front: In fed men, a 48-hour IGF-I infusion cut spontaneous GH pulse amplitude by 77 percent versus saline. In made-up numbers, if saline-period pulse amplitude was 8 ng per mL, what was it during IGF-I? Does the experiment show where IGF-I acted?
cards.back: 8 x 0.23 = 1.84, about 1.8 ng per mL. No: increased hypothalamic somatostatin was an inference from hormone responses; portal blood was not sampled.
cards.quote: The authors favoured increased hypothalamic somatostatin, an inference from hormone responses; nobody sampled portal blood.
cards.section: The IGF-I infusion experiment

cards.front: In young adults, delaying sleep by about three hours moved the night-time GH peak with sleep, and the peak did not track glucose, insulin or cortisol. What does this argue against, and what does it not show?
cards.back: It argues against a clock or the overnight fall in glucose setting the rise. It does not show the hypothalamic mechanism, that the pattern holds at every age, or that glucose never regulates GH.
cards.quote: If a clock or the overnight fall in glucose set the rise, delaying sleep should leave the peak in place.
cards.section: The 1968 sleep study

cards.front: Later deconvolution of naturally secreted GH gave a half-life of about 15 minutes. With that value, what would a 12 ng per mL pulse read 60 minutes after secretion stops, and what does that imply for one random sample?
cards.back: 60 / 15 = 4 half-lives: 12 x 2^-4 = 0.75 ng per mL, versus about 2.6 at a 27-minute half-life. Faster clearance makes one sample depend even more on timing relative to the pulse.
cards.quote: Later deconvolution of naturally secreted GH in healthy adults gave shorter values, about 15 minutes.
cards.section: How fast GH clears

cards.front: After treatment for hyperthyroidism, free T4 is normal but TSH is still suppressed. Does this pair prove ongoing thyroid autonomy?
cards.back: No. TSH can stay suppressed for weeks to months after treatment; the pair rule describes a settled axis.
cards.quote: After a hyperthyroid patient is treated, TSH can stay suppressed for weeks to months while free T4 is already normal or low.
cards.section: When the pair rule is silent or fooled

cards.front: How can hypothalamic hypothyroidism mimic primary thyroid failure on a TSH and free T4 pair?
cards.back: Immunoreactive TSH can be mildly high but poorly bioactive. The assay reports the antibody's view, not the receptor's.
cards.quote: immunoreactive TSH can be mildly high but poorly bioactive, which mimics the opposite-direction pattern of thyroid failure
cards.section: When the pair rule is silent or fooled

cards.front: The ACTH receptor (MC2R) needs the accessory protein MRAP to reach the cell surface. A defect in MRAP leaves the adrenal unable to answer ACTH. Predict the cortisol-ACTH pair and how it is classified.
cards.back: Low cortisol with high ACTH: opposite directions, read as primary.
cards.why: "The gland cannot answer ACTH" includes its receptor machinery, so the fault sits in the target gland.
cards.quote: a fault there reads as primary: high ACTH, low cortisol
cards.section: When the pair rule is silent or fooled

cards.front: In a model, gland output is proportional to the trophic hormone, and pituitary output falls as the target hormone to the power 1.6. The target sits at 0.82 times normal. What trophic level would an intact pituitary show, versus a partial loss of drive?
cards.back: Intact pituitary: 0.82^-1.6, about 1.37 times normal. Partial loss of drive: 0.82 times normal, possibly inside a reference range.
cards.why: This is "inappropriately normal" in numbers: the trophic hormone should be raised but is not.
cards.quote: An intact pituitary facing the same target level would sit at 0.82^-1.6, about 1.37 times normal.
cards.section: When the pair rule is silent or fooled
